summary: Gives guidelines for domain administrators who run a domain name server and look after their part of the hierarchical database. It assumes familiarity with the domain system as described in RFC 1031, RFC 1032, RFC 1034 and RFC 1035.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the how-to manual for the person who keeps the phone book for their own neighborhood of computer names up to date.

subtitle: A hands-on guide to running a domain name server and keeping your zone files in good order.

tldr.problem: People who run a domain server need practical advice on the files it loads, the record formats it holds and sensible values for the numbers inside them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo collects notes on zones, root server lists, resource record formats, TTLs, reverse lookup under IN-ADDR.ARPA, step-by-step chores and a full worked example for the SRI.COM domain.
tldr.outcome: It is a how-to guide rather than a protocol specification, and it assumes you already know the domain system and will consult the domain RFCs for anything advanced.

today: The metadata for RFC 1033 lists its status as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is explicitly a collection of notes for the domain system as defined in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and it defers to those documents for anything advanced.

sections.title: Zones, Boot Files and Root Servers
sections.content:
A domain server needs a few files to get started. The boot or "safety belt" files list possible root servers and name the zone files to load. A zone is a contiguous section of the domain space, usually bounded by administrative boundaries, and its file is made of Resource Records (RRs).

A server may only hold data it is authoritative for. It must not add entries for other domains, except for glue records. The format of the boot file is not standardized and differs between implementations.

When a resolver starts, it reads a list of possible root servers from a file, tries each in turn, asks the first one it reaches for the current list, and replaces its file list with the answer. The memo says root servers do not change often and prints the list as of June 1987.
sections.plainLanguage: A name server starts with a short list of helpers it can ask where to begin. It only keeps pages for its own neighborhood and never writes down names that belong to someone else.

sections.title: Resource Record Format and Names
sections.content:
Every record has the form <name> [<ttl>] [<class>] <type> <data>, with fields separated by white space. A blank name defaults to the previous record's name, a blank class to the last class given, and a blank TTL to the minimum in the SOA record. The RRs are specified in RFC 883 and RFC 973.

Some syntax rules: parentheses group data across lines, a semicolon starts a comment, the asterisk is a wildcard and the at-sign (@) means the current default domain. Order of records is not preserved or guaranteed, and case is kept but ignored in comparisons and lookups.

A domain name is a sequence of labels separated by dots. An absolute name ends with a period; a relative name does not, and the default domain is appended. The domain system allows any 8-bit character in a label, but because other protocols such as SMTP are stricter, the memo recommends only A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash and underscore in host names.

The class of interest for TCP/IP users is IN, and a zone file should hold records of only one class.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry in the phone book has a name, how long to remember it, and the answer. If you leave a part blank, it copies the line above, like writing ditto marks.

sections.title: TTLs and the SOA Record
sections.content:
The TTL is the number of seconds a resolver may use data before asking your server again. Too low and your server is loaded with repeat requests; too high and changes spread slowly. The memo suggests high values, anywhere from a day (86400) to a week (604800), lowered to between an hour and a day before a planned change and then raised again. All RRs with the same name, class and type should have the same TTL.

The SOA (Start Of Authority) record marks the start of a zone, and there should be one per zone. Its fields are the origin host, a responsible-person mailbox (with the at-sign replaced by a dot), and five numbers.

  • serial: the version of the zone file, incremented on every change.
  • refresh: how often a secondary checks the primary; 3600 is suggested.
  • retry: how long to wait after a failed check; 600 is suggested.
  • expire: the limit for using data without a refresh; 3600000, about 42 days, is suggested.
  • minimum: the minimum TTL; at least a day, 86400, is suggested.
sections.plainLanguage: The TTL is how long you may trust a note before checking again. Short means lots of checking, long means slow news, so pick a sensible time and shorten it just before a change.

sections.title: Common Record Types
sections.content:
The memo describes the commonly used types: SOA, NS, A, CNAME, HINFO, WKS, MX and PTR.

  • NS names a machine that provides service for a domain. There should be one per server, and the server need not live inside the domain. NS records exist in both the delegating zone and the domain itself.
  • A holds an address in dotted decimal form, one record per address of a host. A glue A record is needed in the delegating server when the name server is inside the delegated domain.
  • CNAME maps a nickname to the official name. No other RRs of the same class may be associated with a nickname.
  • HINFO gives two strings, hardware then software, with official values in the Assigned Numbers RFC (RFC 1010 at the time).
  • WKS lists well known services, defined as services on port numbers below 256, for an address and protocol such as TCP or UDP.
  • MX says where mail for a name should go. Preference zero is highest, and equal preferences are allowed. A wildcard MX such as *.FOO.COM. matches anything in FOO.COM but not plain FOO.COM. See RFC 974.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different kinds of phone-book lines: one gives a number, one gives a nickname, one says where to send mail, and one says who to ask about a neighborhood.

sections.title: Reverse Lookup under IN-ADDR.ARPA
sections.content:
Because names are indexed by label, there is no easy way to turn an address back into a host name. The solution is the IN-ADDR.ARPA domain, which has a subdomain per network and uses the four octets of a host address in reverse order. Host SRI-NIC.ARPA at 10.0.0.51 therefore has a PTR record at 51.0.0.10.IN-ADDR.ARPA., and a second one at 73.0.0.26.IN-ADDR.ARPA. for its address 26.0.0.73. PTR records should use official names, not aliases.

Gateways get extra PTR records named by network number alone, with 1, 2 or 3 octets for class A, B or C networks, so that they can be found by network. For the SRI-CSL gateway these include 10.IN-ADDR.ARPA., 18.128.IN-ADDR.ARPA. and 33.12.192.IN-ADDR.ARPA..
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you look up a name to find a number. The reverse book lets you start from the number and find the name, and it writes the number backwards so it can be filed neatly.

sections.title: Chores, Complaints and the SRI Example
sections.content:
The memo gives checklists. To add a subdomain: set up the new server or zone file, add an NS record for each of its servers to the parent zone, and add any needed glue. To add a host: add an entry for each address, optionally CNAME, HINFO, WKS and MX records, and the reverse IN-ADDR entry for each address. Deleting reverses these steps, and gateways also need their gateway-location PTR records added or removed.

For problems caused by someone else's name server, the suggested order is to complain privately to the responsible person named in the SOA record, then publicly, then ask the NIC for the contact, then complain to the parent domain authorities, and finally ask the parent to excommunicate the domain.

The long example sets up SRI.COM with subdomains CSL and ISTC, served by the same pair of servers, and shows the boot file, root list and each zone file. The appendix shows the same boot and cache files in the BIND form, named.boot and named.ca. The memo notes that the examples do not necessarily match actual data in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The booklet has a to-do list for adding or removing a name, a polite ladder of what to do if a neighbor's book is wrong, and a full sample book so you can copy the style.
